t.yen giang stake yard@20.9,106.8:
Twice in Vietnamese history, the tide at the mouth of the Bạch Đằng river decided the fate of the country. In 938, Ngô Quyền defeated a Southern Han fleet by planting iron-tipped stakes in the riverbed, hidden at high tide, then luring the enemy ships upstream and waiting for the water to fall. In 1288, during the third Mongol invasion of Đại Việt, the general Trần Hưng Đạo used the same trick against the fleet of Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty, trapping and destroying it. In the fields around Quảng Yên, archaeologists have found rows of those ancient wooden stakes, still standing in the mud, and the Yên Giang stake yard is one of the sites where you can see them preserved.

The area is part of a landscape shaped by water: rice paddies, fishponds, mangroves and the wide estuary where several rivers meet the Gulf of Tonkin. A short ride east lies Hạ Long Bay, with its thousands of limestone islands rising from the sea, and the industrial port city of Haiphong is just across the river to the south. Inland, near Uông Bí, Yên Tử mountain was the retreat of the Trần king Trần Nhân Tông, who abdicated to become a monk and founded the Trúc Lâm school of Zen; pilgrims still climb to its pagodas.

Riding here means dealing with Vietnamese traffic: a dense stream of scooters, trucks and buses, with lots of horn and little lane discipline. Motorcycles are banned from the expressways, so you will use the national and provincial roads, which are busy but usually well surfaced. The countryside roads along the dykes and between the paddies are quieter, though narrow, with buffalo, bicycles and children on their way to school. The weather is hot and humid in summer, with typhoons possible from July to October; winter can be cool, damp and misty.

Uông Bí, eleven kilometres away, and Haiphong have plenty of fuel, food and accommodation, and every village has small petrol stations and noodle shops. Try bánh đa cua, a crab noodle soup from Haiphong, or fresh seafood in Quảng Yên. Bring a good rain jacket, keep your wits about you and enjoy the chaos.
t.vinh nghiem pagoda@21.2,106.3:
In the countryside of Bắc Giang province, in northern Vietnam, about fifty kilometres north-east of Hanoi, the Vinh Nghiem Pagoda stands by the Thương river, surrounded by rice fields and villages. It is one of the oldest and most important Buddhist centres in Vietnam, associated with the Trúc Lâm school of Zen Buddhism, founded in the thirteenth century by King Trần Nhân Tông, who abdicated to become a monk.

The pagoda's greatest treasure is its collection of woodblocks, over three thousand carved wooden blocks used to print Buddhist scriptures, dating mainly from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. They were recognised by UNESCO's Memory of the World Programme for Asia and the Pacific in 2012. The pagoda buildings, with their curved tiled roofs and wooden pillars, are arranged around courtyards with gardens and ponds, and the atmosphere is peaceful, especially in the early morning when monks chant.

Riding in northern Vietnam is lively. The roads around Hanoi are crowded with motorbikes, trucks, buses and cars, and traffic follows its own rules: horns are used constantly, and vehicles weave in and out. Foreigners need a valid licence recognised in Vietnam. Beyond the city, the roads through the countryside are calmer, passing rice fields, villages and markets. The climate is humid, with hot summers and a monsoon season from May to September, and cool, damp winters. Spring and autumn are the best times to ride.

Bắc Giang, about fifteen kilometres away, is a city with fuel, shops and restaurants, and Hanoi has all services. Fuel stations are common along the main roads. Vietnamese food is a delight: phở, noodle soup, bánh mì, filled baguettes, and bún chả, grilled pork with noodles, a Hanoi specialty. Bắc Giang is famous for its lychees, harvested in early summer. Visiting Vinh Nghiem in the early morning, with mist over the rice fields and the sound of chanting from the pagoda, is a peaceful start to the day.
t.thanh mai pagoda@21.2,106.5:
In the late thirteenth century, a Vietnamese king who had twice helped drive back Mongol invasions gave up his throne, put on a monk's robe and founded a Zen school of his own. Trần Nhân Tông's Trúc Lâm school, the Bamboo Grove sect, became the most distinctly Vietnamese form of Buddhism, and the temples connected with it are scattered across the hills of the north-east, from Yên Tử mountain to Côn Sơn and Kiếp Bạc. Thanh Mai pagoda, on a forested slope in the Chí Linh area, is one of these places, associated with the early patriarchs of the school, and it belongs to the Yên Tử, Vĩnh Nghiêm, Côn Sơn and Kiếp Bạc complex that UNESCO listed in 2025.

The pagoda sits among old trees, with stone steps, stupas and halls that have been rebuilt and restored over the centuries, and the setting has the calm, green, slightly misty quality that suits a Zen retreat. Pilgrims climb up for festivals, especially in spring after the lunar new year, when the hills fill with incense smoke and visitors.

Riding in northern Vietnam is an experience of its own. Traffic on the main roads is dense and chaotic, with motorbikes in their thousands, trucks, buses and cars all sharing the road on terms that are not always obvious to a newcomer. Patience, defensive riding and a liberal use of the horn are part of the culture. The roads up into the hills toward the pagodas are narrower, steeper and quieter, winding through forest and lychee orchards, with variable surfaces and the odd buffalo.

Fuel is easy to find in towns and along main roads, with small stations and roadside sellers in every village. Chí Linh is the nearest town with full services, and the cities of Hải Dương and Bắc Giang are within reach. Food is a joy: phở for breakfast, bún chả, grilled pork with noodles, fresh spring rolls, and the lychees of the region in early summer, sold by the basket along the roads.

The best time to come is autumn, from October to December, when the weather is dry and comfortable. Spring is busy with festivals and can be drizzly, and summer is hot, humid and rainy. Climb the steps slowly in the early morning, when mist hangs in the trees, and listen for the temple bell carrying across the hills.
t.bo da pagoda@21.2,106.1:
Bổ Đà is a pagoda that was built from the earth up, quite literally. Its long perimeter walls are made of rammed earth, mixed with broken pottery and tiles, a traditional technique that has kept them standing for centuries, and inside lies one of the most remarkable features of any Vietnamese temple: a garden of more than a thousand stupas, the tombs of monks who lived and died here, standing in rows among the trees. The pagoda, on a hill in Việt Yên in Bắc Giang province, is also famous for its collection of wooden printing blocks carved with Buddhist texts, a treasure of Vietnamese woodblock printing.

The site is associated with the Lâm Tế school of Buddhism and has been a centre of learning and pilgrimage since at least the seventeenth century, with the main halls rebuilt over the years. The atmosphere is calm and earthy, with the scent of incense, moss-covered walls and the sound of monks chanting in the morning.

Bắc Ninh, across the river, is the heartland of quan họ, a style of call-and-response folk singing between groups of young men and women, recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage. The village of Đông Hồ, nearby, is famous for its woodblock folk paintings, printed on paper made from tree bark with natural colours, especially popular at the lunar new year.

Riding in this area is busy, flat and full of incident. Roads around Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang carry heavy traffic, including trucks serving the many industrial parks that have grown here in recent years, and motorbikes swarm at every junction. Smaller roads through villages and rice fields are calmer, but still demand constant attention, with bicycles, livestock and children playing in the road.

Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere. Try Vietnamese coffee, strong and sweet with condensed milk, or egg coffee, a Hanoi invention, and local dishes like bánh cuốn, steamed rice rolls. Come in autumn, when the weather is dry and pleasant, or spring, when festivals bring life to the temples. Summers are hot and wet. Walk slowly through the stupa garden, past the weathered towers in their rows, and feel the presence of the generations of monks who made this place their home.
t.central sector of the imperial citadel o:
In 1010 the Vietnamese king Lý Thái Tổ moved his capital to the banks of the Red River and named it Thăng Long, Ascending Dragon, after he is said to have seen a dragon rising from the water. The city grew up around the royal citadel, and for most of the next eight centuries it was the political heart of Vietnam. The Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, in the middle of modern Hanoi, preserves layers of this history, from the foundations of palaces excavated beneath the ground to buildings of the Nguyễn dynasty and the French colonial era. It was listed by UNESCO in 2010, the year Hanoi celebrated its thousandth anniversary.

The highlights include the Đoan Môn gate, a grand stone gateway with five arches, and the Kính Thiên palace foundations with their carved dragon staircase. Across the road, at 18 Hoàng Diệu, an archaeological excavation has revealed wells, foundations, roof tiles and ceramics from many dynasties. More recent history is here too: a bunker known as D67, used by the North Vietnamese military command during the war, with maps and telephones still in place. Nearby stands the Hanoi Flag Tower, built in the early nineteenth century.

The citadel is close to Ba Đình Square, where Hồ Chí Minh declared independence in 1945 and where his mausoleum now stands. The Temple of Literature, Vietnam's first university, is a short ride away, and the Old Quarter, with its narrow streets named after the goods once sold there, is a few minutes further.

Riding in Hanoi is an experience you will not forget. The streets are packed with motorbikes and scooters, moving in a constant flow that seems chaotic but has its own logic. Go slowly, stay predictable, use the horn as locals do, and do not make sudden moves. Foreigners need a valid licence recognised in Vietnam, and the rules about international permits are specific, so check before you ride. Outside the city, the roads north into the mountains are some of the most spectacular in Asia.

Fuel is everywhere, and so is food. Try phở for breakfast, bún chả for lunch, and a glass of iced coffee with condensed milk at any time. The weather is hot and humid in summer, cool and damp in winter; autumn, from September to November, is the most pleasant season.
t.ngoa van hermitage pagoda relic cluster@:
In 1293 the Vietnamese king Trần Nhân Tông, who had led his country to victory against two Mongol invasions, gave up his throne and became a monk. He retreated to the mountains of Yên Tử, east of Hanoi, and founded the Trúc Lâm, or Bamboo Forest, school of Zen Buddhism, a distinctly Vietnamese tradition that still flourishes today. In his final years he lived at a hermitage on the mountain of Ngọa Vân, and it was there that he died in 1308. The pagodas, stupas and relics scattered across the ridge form part of the complex of sites connected with Yên Tử and the Trúc Lâm school, which has recently been recognised by UNESCO.

The hermitage sits high on a forested ridge in Đông Triều, in Quảng Ninh province, reached by a steep path and stone steps through the trees. Along the way are small shrines, old stupas and a stone sculpture said to represent the reclining king. The atmosphere is peaceful and spiritual, with the sound of wind in the trees and the occasional bell. In the spring festival season, after Tết, thousands of pilgrims climb the mountains of Yên Tử to pray, and the paths and roads become very crowded.

The landscape is a mix of forested mountains, limestone hills, rice paddies and coal-mining towns; Quảng Ninh is Vietnam's coal province, and the mines and industry are visible in places. Not far away is Hạ Long Bay, with its thousands of limestone islands rising from the sea, one of the most famous sights in Asia.

The riding to get here is varied. The main roads from Hanoi towards Hạ Long are busy, with heavy truck traffic, and a new expressway carries much of the long-distance traffic, though motorcycles are not allowed on expressways in Vietnam. The smaller roads into the mountains are narrow and winding, with steep gradients and variable surfaces. Watch for buses, trucks, scooters and livestock.

The nearest towns with full services are Đông Triều and Uông Bí, both with fuel, shops and restaurants. Try the local seafood from the coast, or a bowl of phở. The weather is hot and humid in summer, with heavy rain and typhoons possible; winter is cool and damp, with mist on the mountains. Autumn and spring are the most pleasant seasons for riding.
t.chua lan pagoda@21.1,106.7:
The lowlands where the Bach Dang river meets the sea in northern Vietnam are a place of legends and battles, and the pagodas scattered across this landscape carry centuries of history. Chua Lan Pagoda stands in Quang Ninh province on the low ground south of Uong Bi, between the Yen Tu hills and the port of Haiphong, surrounded by rice fields, fishponds and villages. Like many rural pagodas in northern Vietnam, it is a place of worship, community and memory, with incense-filled halls, statues of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and old trees in the courtyard. The region is associated with the Truc Lam school of Zen Buddhism, founded by the Tran dynasty king Tran Nhan Tong in the thirteenth century at nearby Yen Tu mountain.

The Bach Dang river is famous in Vietnamese history for three great battles, the most celebrated in 1288, when Tran Hung Dao defeated a Mongol fleet by planting iron-tipped wooden stakes in the riverbed, then luring the ships in at high tide so that they were impaled as the water fell. The remains of these stakes have been found in the area, including at the Yen Giang stake yard near Quang Yen, and they are now a historic site. The story is a source of great national pride.

Riding in this area means dealing with Vietnamese traffic: a constant flow of scooters, trucks, buses and cars, with horns used freely and lane discipline loose. The main roads between Haiphong, Uong Bi and Ha Long are busy and sometimes chaotic, but the side roads through the villages and rice fields are quieter, with narrow lanes, bridges and the occasional water buffalo. Surfaces vary, and flooding can be an issue in the rainy season. The hills of Yen Tu, to the north, offer better riding, with winding roads up into the forest.

Uong Bi, about ten kilometres away, has fuel stations, markets and restaurants, and Haiphong, further south, is a major city with everything. Food in this coastal region is excellent, with seafood, banh da cua, a crab noodle soup from Haiphong, and fresh spring rolls. Remove your shoes and dress modestly when entering the pagoda. Light some incense if you wish, sit quietly in the courtyard, and enjoy a moment of calm before heading back into the traffic.
t.king chu cavern@21.0,106.5:
In the delta country east of Hanoi the land is mostly flat, a patchwork of rice paddies and ponds, so when limestone hills rise abruptly out of it they feel like a different world. Kinh Môn, in Hải Dương province, is one of those places, a small range of karst hills pitted with caves, and the Kinh Chủ cave, which I have placed under the name on the map, is one of them. Caves in northern Vietnam are often turned into shrines, with Buddha statues and incense in the dim light, and visitors come both for the religion and for the cool air inside.

Do not expect a quiet wilderness. This is a working landscape, and cement plants have been cut into these limestone hills for generations, so dust, trucks and industrial sites sit alongside temples and rice fields. Even so, the contrast is memorable: a monk's chant in a cave, the green glare of paddies outside, and the river Kinh Thầy running muddy and busy with barges. The pagoda in the same ride, Thanh Mai, is associated with one of Vietnam's Buddhist traditions, and you will often find locals leaving offerings there on feast days.

For riding, northern Vietnam rewards the patient. Highway 5 between Hanoi and Haiphong is busy and loud, full of motorbikes, lorries and buses, and the secondary roads are often better for the experience, with village markets, dikes and bridges over canals. Expect surprises: a water buffalo on the road, a sudden stall of fruit, a crowd of schoolchildren on bicycles. Surfaces are usually paved but can be uneven, and rain turns the shoulders to mud. Spring is mild and damp, summer hot and wet with typhoons possible, and October to December is generally the most comfortable.

Hải Dương, about twenty-one kilometres away, is large enough for petrol stations, hotels and restaurants, and it is famous for a mung-bean cake called bánh đậu xanh that you will see in boxes in shops everywhere. Fill up before you head out to the hills, since village pumps can be few. Take a head torch if you plan to go into the cave, wear shoes with grip, and leave a small offering or donation if the keepers ask.
Ha Long means descending dragon, and the legend says a dragon family came down from heaven to spit out jewels that became the islands, which is as good an explanation as any for nearly two thousand limestone towers rising from green water. UNESCO listed the bay in the 1990s for its scenery and its geology, and the Cát Bà archipelago to the south joins the same landscape of steep karst islands, hidden lagoons and floating fishing villages. The scale is hard to describe: islands shaped like teeth, like ships, like sleeping animals, all standing in a calm, jade-coloured sea.

Cát Bà Island, the largest in the group, is also a biosphere reserve, with forest, mangroves and caves, and it is home to the Cát Bà langur, one of the rarest primates on earth, which you are most unlikely to see. The local economy runs on tourism and fishing, and the bay is busy with tour boats, so do not expect solitude, but you can often find calm if you go early or in the shoulder seasons. The ride here is a different kind of adventure from the mountain passes: you are on the edge of the sea, and the road is a way to see it.

Roads around Hạ Long are good by Vietnamese standards, with a coastal road past the Bãi Cháy waterfront and over a long bridge, and heavy traffic in the town. The approach from Hanoi is by expressway, which is fast but monotonous, and the real riding pleasure comes when you leave it for the smaller roads. Tourist season brings congestion, especially at weekends, and the weather matters: typhoons can arrive between June and October, and sea mist in late winter can reduce views to nothing. October to April is generally the better window.

Hạ Long has fuel, restaurants and hotels in abundance, with fresh seafood served along the front, including grilled squid and a local fish cake called chả mực. Boat trips to the islands depart from the harbours, and the ferry to Cát Bà leaves from nearby ports, so check schedules and whether you can take a motorcycle aboard. Book ahead in high season, since the bay is very popular, and carry sun cream and a light waterproof.
t.con son pagoda@21.2,106.4:
Côn Sơn lies in the pine-covered hills of Chí Linh, north-east of Hanoi, on the border of Hải Dương province, and it carries two of the great names of Vietnamese history. In the thirteenth century the Trần dynasty beat back three Mongol invasions, and its monks and commanders left a trail of temples, of which Côn Sơn, Kiếp Bạc and the sacred mountain of Yên Tử are the best known. Trúc Lâm, the Vietnamese Zen school founded by King Trần Nhân Tông, who gave up his throne to become a monk, has one of its centres here.

A century later, the scholar and strategist Nguyễn Trãi, who helped Lê Lợi drive the Chinese Ming army out of Vietnam in the 1420s, grew up and later retired here, and wrote poems about the pines and the stream. The pagoda, shaded by old trees, holds a stone stele and shrines to the Zen patriarchs and to Nguyễn Trãi, and a path leads uphill through the forest to a stone seat where the poet is said to have sat. The cluster of Yên Tử, Vĩnh Nghiêm and Côn Sơn, Kiếp Bạc was listed by UNESCO in 2025.

The nearby towns are Cung Kiệm, with a big population in the surrounding area, and Bắc Giang, a city of over fifty thousand, so fuel, noodles and tea are never far. The roads of northern Vietnam are busy, with motorbikes, trucks and buses all sharing the lanes, and drivers use the horn constantly, so the rider needs a calm head and wide eyes. Rules for foreign visitors on motorcycles are complicated, with licence recognition and paperwork, so check them before you go.

The pleasure is in the hills away from the main roads, with small lanes running through lychee orchards, rice fields and bamboo, and a haze that turns the light soft. The best seasons are autumn and early spring, with festival days in the first months of the lunar year, when the temple fills with pilgrims. Summers are hot, humid and stormy. Take a bowl of pho or banh cuon and a glass of iced tea, and walk up under the pines.
t.nham duong pagoda@21.0,106.5:
Out in the hills of Chí Linh, in Hai Duong province east of Hanoi, the land crumples into low forested ridges after the flat Red River delta, and this is where Nham Duong sits among the trees. The pagoda belongs to a cluster of temples tied to the Trần dynasty and its home-grown school of Zen, the Trúc Lâm tradition, whose three patriarchs taught in these hills during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Thanh Mai, the other pagoda on the same ride, is part of that story too.

Vietnamese pagodas like this are working places, not museums. Incense smoke drifts across the courtyard, monks in grey robes sweep the steps, and families come with offerings of fruit and flowers. The roof lines curl upward, the beams are dark wood, and the carved dragon heads and lotus patterns have been repainted and repaired over the centuries. Expect a hush that surprises you after the roar of the roads. Take your shoes off at the main hall, keep your voice low, and keep shoulders and knees covered.

The ride from Hanoi or Haiphong is pleasant but busy in the delta stretch. National roads are full of lorries, minibuses and scooters, so give yourself time. Once you reach the hills the traffic thins, the road narrows, and lychee orchards line the slopes. Chí Linh and the nearby district of Thanh Hà are known for lychees, which ripen in early summer, and you will see stalls on every verge in June. Winters are cool and often grey with drizzle, and the coolest months can seem surprisingly cold for the tropics.

Hải Dương, twenty-four kilometres away, is the practical choice for fuel and a proper meal, and Uông Bí is nearly as close on the other side. Before the hills there is rarely a long wait between petrol stations. Try the local mung bean cakes from Hải Dương as a snack on the road, and bring a little cash for incense and donations at the temple.
t.ha giang@22.8,105.0:
Ha Giang is where Vietnam runs out of country. The city lies on the Lô River in the far north, just a short ride from the Chinese border, and it is the gateway to one of the most dramatic road circuits in Southeast Asia. Beyond the last streets, the road lifts into the Dong Van Karst Plateau, a UNESCO Global Geopark since 2010, where limestone peaks and gorges crowd every horizon and terraces of corn and rice climb the hillsides.

The loop is about three hundred and fifty kilometres, normally ridden over three or four days, and it deserves that time. The road climbs through Quản Bạ, where the hills are shaped like twin breasts, then Yên Minh and Đồng Văn, the old stone town where a market draws Hmong, Lô Lô and Tay people in traditional clothes on Sunday mornings. Near Sà Phìn is the palace of the Vương family, a Hmong clan that once ruled the region. The surface is tarmac for most of the way, but it is narrow and steep, with hairpins, blind bends and sudden gravel, and heavy fog can appear in minutes. Landslides are common in the wet season from May to September.

The great moment is the Mã Pí Lèng Pass, where the road is cut into a cliff high above the Nho Quế River, which runs in a green ribbon at the bottom of the Tu San canyon, among the deepest in Southeast Asia. The views are staggering, with layers of mountain fading into the distance, and the traffic, mainly local trucks and motorbikes, is slow. Autumn brings buckwheat flowers in pink and white on the plateau, usually in October and November, and the terraces glow gold in September.

Fuel is available in Ha Giang city and in every larger town on the loop, and small roadside stalls sell petrol in bottles in the villages. Homestays with simple meals, rice wine and a warm bed are the best way to sleep. Take warm clothes, since nights at altitude are cold, and rain gear all year. Check the weather before you go, and take it slowly, because the road does not forgive speed.
t.quan ba heaven@23.1,105.0:
The Heaven Gate, Cổng Trời in Vietnamese, is the pass above Quản Bạ, where the road tops a ridge at about fifteen hundred metres and the whole Dong Van Karst Plateau opens beneath it. Below, a valley of green rice terraces and small fields is dotted with the humped outlines of limestone hills, and in the middle sits the pair of round green mounds known as Núi Đôi, the Twin Mountains, which local people call the Fairy's Bosom. On a clear morning, mist lies in the hollows and the hills float above it.

This is the far north of Vietnam, a few kilometres from the Chinese border, and the country is mountain, rock and weather. The Dong Van Karst Plateau is a UNESCO Global Geopark, recognised in 2010, a high landscape of grey limestone, deep gorges and ancient fossils, and it is home to a mosaic of ethnic groups, including the Hmong, Tay, Dao and Lo Lo. Villagers farm every scrap of soil, planting maize between the rocks, and weekly markets bring colourful traditional costumes. The nearest big town is Hà Giang, about twenty-six kilometres back, where you should fill the tank and check the bike.

The Ha Giang Loop is a famous adventure for riders, and this pass is one of its first great moments. The road is a ribbon of switchbacks cut into the mountainside, mostly paved but narrow, with blind curves, potholes, sudden fog and trucks and buses taking the middle of the road. Take it gently, use the horn at corners and watch for livestock. In the rainy season, from about May to September, landslides and slick surfaces are common, while autumn and spring offer clearer weather, though cold mornings.

Pack layers, a rain jacket and a spare phone battery, as it gets chilly at altitude. Buy water and snacks in town, and look for small roadside stalls selling sweet corn and tea. At the pass there are stalls and viewpoints, and a short stop gives you the best view of the Twin Mountains. Local guesthouses in Quản Bạ and Tam Sơn serve simple, tasty meals, and the Hmong market days make the village lively. Early starts help avoid cloud and traffic.
t.ma pi leng pass@23.3,105.4:
Mã Pí Lèng is the great pass of the Ha Giang Loop, a road cut along the side of a vast gorge on the way between Đồng Văn and Mèo Vạc, and it earns its reputation in the first minute. At about fifteen hundred metres, the road clings to a cliff hundreds of metres above the Nho Quế River, which winds through a sheer, green-black canyon far below, often described as one of the deepest in Southeast Asia. The sides drop away on one hand, the mountain climbs on the other, and the colour of the river, a clear jade turquoise on a good day, is unforgettable.

The road has a story that matters. It is known as the Happiness Road, and it was built by hand between 1959 and 1965 by thousands of young volunteers and local labourers from many ethnic groups, who hung from ropes to drill and blast the cliff face with little more than hammers and dynamite, working for months at a time. A monument at the pass recognises their effort, and some of those who built it died in the work. Today it is a paved, if narrow, road, with viewing points, tea stalls and small cafés where you can sit and look across the gorge.

For a rider, the pass is a thrilling, careful ride. The bends are tight and often blind, the road is shared with trucks, buses, scooters and livestock, and fog can appear suddenly, cutting visibility to a few metres. Rain makes the surface treacherous. Go slowly, stay on your side, and use your horn before blind corners. Mornings are often clearest, and the best light is just after sunrise, when the sun burns off the mist. The road is frequently crowded with tour groups at midday.

Carry water, warm clothes and a rain jacket, as temperatures can drop sharply. Local food in the nearby towns includes thắng cố, a hearty horse or beef stew, and buckwheat cakes. In autumn, the buckwheat flowers bloom pink across the hills, and the days are crisp and clear, making it the best season.
t.cao bang@22.7,106.3:
Cao Bang is a market town in the far northeast of Vietnam, hemmed in by limestone mountains and only a short distance from the Chinese border. The Bang Giang River winds through the town, and beyond it a landscape of karst pinnacles, caves and rice terraces stretches in every direction. It is a quiet provincial capital, home to Tay, Nung and Hmong people, with a bustling covered market and food stalls serving the local specialties, including roast duck, rice-paper rolls and sticky rice with colored dyes.

History here is deep and political. In 1941, after thirty years abroad, Ho Chi Minh returned to Vietnam through a cave at Pac Bo, in the hills near the border, and used the cave as a base to organize the independence movement. The site, with its stream, rock table and surrounding forest, is now a national monument. Earlier, the Mac dynasty, driven from Hanoi, held out in Cao Bang for decades in the late sixteenth century. The area is now a UNESCO Global Geopark, recognized for its geology and limestone landscape.

The big attraction is the Ban Gioc waterfall, about eighty kilometers northeast, where the Quay Son River tumbles in broad tiers over limestone steps, forming the border with China. It is among the largest waterfalls in the world to straddle an international border, and the best time to see it is September and October, when water is high and the rice fields around are golden. Nearby, the Nguom Ngao cave is a vast, lit cavern of stalactites. The road there runs through karst scenery, with pointed hills rising from the paddies, and gentle curves along the river.

Cao Bang has fuel, food and several hotels, and the roads are generally decent but narrow, with trucks, motorbikes and animals, so slow down for corners. The mountain passes on the road from Hanoi, long and winding, can be misty and slippery. The best months are September to November, with clear skies and mild weather, and spring, when the hills are green. Summer is hot, wet and prone to landslides, and winter brings cold, damp fog. Carry some cash, as card payment is rare, and do not ride at night if you can help it.
t.hanoi@21.0,105.8:
Hanoi is a city you ride into with your elbows tucked in. On the Red River delta, a thousand years after it was first made a royal capital, it has an Old Quarter where the streets still carry the names of old guilds, silk, silver, tin, hats, and in front of every door a few plastic stools and a pot of something steaming. The motorbike is the language of the place: families of four, whole shop windows and live ducks all travel on two wheels, and the flow of traffic at a roundabout looks chaotic until you notice how courteous it is. Hold your line, signal with your eyes, and move steadily.

The city's centre of gravity is Hoan Kiem Lake, the Lake of the Returned Sword, named for the legend of a king who handed back a magic blade to a giant turtle. Nearby, the Temple of Literature, founded in 1070 for Confucian learning, is a quiet courtyard of old trees and stone tortoises. French colonial boulevards, yellow villas and the opera house recall the century of colonial rule, and the mausoleum of Ho Chi Minh, on Ba Dinh Square, draws long queues. For breakfast, find a pavement stall for phở, and for something odder, egg coffee, whipped yolk over strong brew.

The route out toward Moc Chau heads west and north-west across the delta, then climbs into the limestone mountains of Hoa Binh province. The first hour is slow, with trucks, towns and heavy traffic, so leave early. Once you are past Hoa Binh the road begins to climb, with long bends over passes and wide views over valleys of rice and tea, and the Da River below, dammed into a long reservoir. Mist is common on the ridges, and the road can be slick with wet clay after rain.

Fuel stations are everywhere in the Hanoi region, and in the mountain towns there are enough to keep you moving, although it is worth topping up before the long climbs. Autumn and spring are the most pleasant seasons, with clear air and mild temperatures. Summer is hot, wet and humid, and winter can be surprisingly cold on the high ridges, where a thermal layer is welcome.
t.hoa yen pagoda relic cluster@21.2,106.7:
Yên Tử is the sacred mountain of Vietnamese Buddhism, rising to a little over a thousand metres above the coastal plain of Quảng Ninh province, and Hoa Yên Pagoda sits partway up its slopes, among old trees and stone steps, on the pilgrim route to the summit. The mountain's fame goes back to King Trần Nhân Tông, who defeated the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century and then, at the height of his power, gave up the throne, became a monk and retired to Yên Tử, where he founded the Trúc Lâm school of Zen. It became the only uniquely Vietnamese school of Buddhism, and the mountain has been a pilgrimage site ever since.

The ascent is traditionally made on foot, up thousands of steps through forest of bamboo, pine and ancient trees, with pagodas, shrines and stupas along the way, including a garden of stone stupas containing the relics of monks. At the top, a small bronze pagoda sits on the summit rock, often wrapped in cloud. Today there are cable cars for those who prefer, but many pilgrims still walk. During the spring festival, starting in the first lunar month after Tết, the mountain is crowded with tens of thousands of visitors.

The landscape around Yên Tử is green and mountainous, with coal mining towns at its foot, since Quảng Ninh is Vietnam's main coal region. Uông Bí is the nearest city, and the industrial scenery can be a shock after the serenity of the mountain. Ha Long Bay, with its famous limestone islands, is less than an hour's ride to the east.

Riding in Vietnam means joining a river of motorbikes, and the roads around Uông Bí and towards Hải Phòng are busy, noisy and chaotic, with trucks carrying coal and cement. Ride defensively, follow the flow, and keep your horn handy. The road up to the base of Yên Tử is good, climbing gently through the forest. Fuel is easy to find in Uông Bí and along the main roads, as are phở stalls, rice dishes and strong Vietnamese coffee. Summer is hot and humid with typhoons; winter, from December to February, is cool and often misty, which can be beautiful on the mountain but slippery on the roads.
t.yen tu vinh nghiem con son@21.1,106.5:
In the late thirteenth century, a Vietnamese king who had twice helped drive back the Mongol armies gave up his throne, climbed the mountain of Yen Tu and became a monk. Tran Nhan Tong founded the Truc Lam school of Zen Buddhism there, a uniquely Vietnamese form that combined meditation with engagement in the world, and Yen Tu became the holiest mountain in northern Vietnam. Together with the pagoda of Vinh Nghiem, which preserves thousands of woodblocks used for printing Buddhist texts, and the Con Son and Kiep Bac relics, associated with the scholar Nguyen Trai and the general Tran Hung Dao, the complex was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2025.

The pilgrimage up Yen Tu is a huge event in the first months of the lunar year, when hundreds of thousands of people climb the stone paths and stairs through bamboo and pine forest to the pagodas and the bronze summit temple, often in the mist. A cable car now takes much of the effort out of the climb. Con Son, near Chi Linh, is a peaceful hill with a pagoda and a lake, and Kiep Bac, next to it, honours Tran Hung Dao, who defeated the Mongol fleet at the Bach Dang river in 1288 by planting stakes in the riverbed and luring the enemy ships onto them at low tide. The Yen Giang stake yard, where some of these stakes have been found, is a short ride away near Quang Yen.

The main road through the region, Highway 18, links Hanoi with Ha Long Bay and the coast, and it is busy with trucks, buses and motorbikes, with dust from quarries and coal mines in places. The smaller roads into the hills around Yen Tu and Con Son are narrower, winding through rice fields, villages and forest, and are much more pleasant. Expect traffic to follow its own logic, with constant horn use and overtaking on all sides.

Uong Bi, the nearest city, has fuel, hotels and restaurants, and there are shops and food stalls at the foot of the mountain. Try a bowl of pho or bun cha in a local eatery, and if you visit during the festival season, be prepared for crowds and a festive, chaotic atmosphere.
t.kiep bac temple@21.2,106.3:
Kiếp Bạc is the place where Vietnam remembers Trần Hưng Đạo, the thirteenth-century general who defeated the Mongols three times. In the 1280s, the armies of Kublai Khan's empire invaded Vietnam, and Trần Hưng Đạo, commanding the forces of the Trần dynasty, used guerrilla tactics, retreat and ambush to wear them down. The most famous victory came in 1288 on the Bạch Đằng river, when he planted iron-tipped stakes in the riverbed and lured the Mongol fleet onto them at low tide. He died in 1300, and the temple at Kiếp Bạc was built where he is said to have had his base.

The temple stands among hills and fields in Hải Dương province, in the Chí Linh district, a green landscape of rice paddies and lychee trees, and it is a place of pilgrimage. Every year, in the eighth month of the lunar calendar, which falls in the autumn, huge crowds arrive for a festival in his honour, with processions, incense, drums and offerings. At other times the courtyards are calm, with old trees, stone tablets and red-lacquered halls, and the atmosphere is more local than touristic.

In Vietnam, the way to travel is by motorbike, and this area is a good one for it. The roads run through a flat, fertile region of the Red River delta, then climb gently into low hills, with plenty of traffic, trucks, buses and scooters, all moving in a loose and flexible flow. Keep your speed down, look out for people and animals stepping out, and be ready for pot holes. In summer, heavy rain and heat make riding uncomfortable, and autumn and spring are the best seasons. The lychee harvest, in June, makes the whole province smell sweet.

Fuel is easy to find on all the main roads, and Chí Linh town has plenty of small restaurants and cafes. Hải Dương is known for its mung bean cake, a sweet crumbly treat that makes a good snack, and for its lychees from Thanh Hà. Dress modestly at the temple, take your shoes off when asked, and treat the offerings with respect. Allow extra time for the busy roads, because distances take longer than the map suggests.
t.thai mieu@21.1,106.6:
This is Trần dynasty country. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the Trần kings ruled Đại Việt from here and from the delta, and they are best remembered for turning back the Mongol armies three times, in 1258, 1285 and 1288, under the general Trần Hưng Đạo. The Thái Miếu, an ancestral temple associated with the dynasty, belongs to this landscape of royal tombs and shrines in the hills near Đông Triều, in Quảng Ninh province, at the northern edge of the Red River delta.

The setting is soft and green: low wooded ridges, rice paddies, ponds with lotus, and village lanes shaded by banyan and bamboo. Not far east rises Yên Tử, the mountain where Trần Nhân Tông, after his reign, withdrew to found the Trúc Lâm school of Vietnamese Zen. The Chùa Lân and Bồ Đà pagodas on neighbouring rides belong to that Buddhist heritage. The air smells of incense, wet earth and burning rice straw, depending on the season.

Quảng Ninh is also coal country, and that colours the ride. Trucks thunder along the main roads, dust hangs over the junctions, and every few kilometres you pass a quarry, a washing plant or a mining town. Then you turn off onto a village road and suddenly everything is quiet. Surfaces are generally paved but patched, and scooters, bicycles, buffalo and chickens share the lane. Ride calmly, keep your speed low in villages, and give right of way to anything larger than you.

The nearest city of any size is Uông Bí, about twenty-five kilometres away, with about sixty thousand people, fuel stations and plenty of noodle shops. Smaller settlements nearer the temple will have tiny roadside stalls and petrol sold from bottles, which works in an emergency but is best avoided. The cooler months from October to March are most pleasant; summer is hot and humid with heavy downpours, and typhoons can disrupt the coast from July to September. Dress respectfully if you step inside the temple grounds.
t.trang an landscape complex@20.3,105.9:
The first view of Trang An catches people out. You step into a rowing boat, an old woman or man takes the oars, often with feet as well as hands, and the boat glides into a cave in a limestone cliff, comes out the other end into a hidden lagoon ringed by green peaks, and slides into another cave, and another, for a couple of hours. The Trang An Landscape Complex, in Ninh Bình province, is a maze of karst towers, flooded valleys, caves and rice fields, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2014 for both natural and cultural value.

The history is substantial. Hoa Lư, a short distance away, was the capital of Vietnam in the tenth century, under the Đinh and early Lê dynasties, when the new state first broke away from centuries of Chinese rule. The kings used the natural fortress of cliffs as a defence, and the temples dedicated to them are still in use. Caves in the area hold evidence of human occupation thousands of years old. Some of the scenes in a recent King Kong film were shot among the cliffs, which gave the place extra fame.

For riders, the main lesson is practical. Ninh Bình is about ninety kilometres south of Hanoi, and motorbikes are banned on the expressways in Vietnam, so you must take the older Highway 1, which is busy with trucks, buses and scooters, noisy, dusty, and slow. The roads around Trang An itself are quiet by comparison, flat and mostly well surfaced, running between rice paddies with karst peaks on every horizon, and a short ride from the boat station leads to quiet lanes along canals. Traffic can be chaotic in the town, and drivers do not always follow rules, so keep your speed down.

Ninh Bình has fuel, markets, guesthouses and many restaurants, and Bỉm Sơn, to the south, is a larger industrial town. The local speciality is goat meat, served in many ways, and com chay, crispy burnt rice, which is eaten with sauces. Boats leave from the visitor centre, tickets are sold in advance, and the trips last two to three hours, with several routes.

The best time is spring and autumn, when the weather is dry, though January and February can be cool and misty, and summers are hot and humid.
t.dong van@23.3,105.4:
Dong Van is a small market town in the far north of Vietnam, close to the Chinese border, and it lies at the heart of a remarkable landscape of limestone. The Dong Van Karst Plateau, a UNESCO Global Geopark, is a high, rocky country of grey peaks, deep gorges and tiny terraced fields, where farmers grow maize and buckwheat in pockets of soil carried by hand and planted between the rocks. At around a thousand metres, the air is cool, mist hangs in the valleys, and the villages are built of stone, with walls and roofs of rough grey slabs.

The old quarter of the town has a row of low, tile-roofed houses from the French colonial period, with a market that fills on Sunday mornings with people from the surrounding hills. The Hmong, Dao, Lolo and Tay minorities come in their traditional dress, in bright embroidery and silver, to trade livestock, vegetables, spices and homemade corn liquor. It is a lively, colourful and slightly chaotic scene, and the steaming pots of noodles and the smoke from grills make it a good place for breakfast. A short way south, in Sa Phin, a mansion built by a Hmong chieftain in the early twentieth century is a fascinating relic.

The road you are riding, the Ha Giang loop, is one of the great motorcycle journeys of Southeast Asia. Between Dong Van and Meo Vac runs the Ma Pi Leng Pass, a narrow road carved along a cliff above the Nho Que River gorge, which lies hundreds of metres below in a deep green ribbon. Hmong workers built it by hand in the 1960s over several years, and it is sometimes called the Happiness Road. The views are tremendous, but the road is steep, narrow and often foggy, with trucks and buses on the bends, so ride slowly and keep right.

Fuel is available in town, though stations in the hills are small and supplies can run short, so fill up whenever you can. The nights are cold, and the best time to visit is autumn, when the buckwheat flowers cover the fields with pink, or spring. Rain turns the roads slick, and landslides are common in the wet season. Many travellers hire a local rider to guide them, which is a sensible choice if you are unfamiliar with the roads. A bowl of hot noodles and a cup of strong coffee at dawn is a good way to begin.
t.meo vac@23.2,105.4:
Meo Vac sits at the edge of the Dong Van Karst Plateau Geopark, near the Chinese border in the far north of Vietnam, and it feels like the end of the map. The town is built on a ridge of grey limestone, among peaks that look like broken teeth, and the road in from the west is the famous Ma Pi Leng Pass, a narrow shelf cut into a cliff above a gorge so deep that the Nho Que River at the bottom is a thin green thread. The pass was part of the Happiness Road, built by thousands of volunteers and local Hmong people over some six years starting in 1959.

The town is known for its Sunday market, when people from the surrounding hills, in the colours of many different ethnic groups, gather to trade livestock, corn spirit, herbs and cloth. Hmong families walk down from villages that are hours away, and the market fills the main street and the old square. It is lively, crowded and generous with samples. Maize and buckwheat are staples of this high country, and in autumn the buckwheat fields burst into pink and white flowers that cover terraces among the rocks.

For a rider, the roads here are as demanding as they are beautiful. Corners are tight and often blind, the surface can be broken, and mist rolls in at any hour. Trucks and buses take the middle of the road, and animals wander freely. Take your time, use the horn on blind bends, and do not ride after dark. The best seasons are autumn, from September to November, when the air is clear, and spring, though the cold and fog of winter can be harsh.

Fuel is available in town, but fill up whenever you can, because pumps in the mountains are far apart and sometimes sell in bottles. Simple eateries serve noodle soup, grilled pork, sticky rice and corn wine, and a bowl of pho in the cold air tastes remarkable. Local guesthouses are friendly, and the evenings are cool and quiet.
t.du gia@22.9,105.2:
Du Gia is a quiet valley village in the north of Ha Giang province, and it makes a gentle end to a ride that has spent days among limestone peaks. The mountains here soften into green hills, rice terraces step down the slopes, and the houses are wooden stilt homes with tiled roofs belonging to Tay, Dao and Hmong families. Smoke rises from kitchen fires in the early morning, and the air smells of woodsmoke, wet earth and ripening rice.

Compared with the great passes farther north, the landscape is intimate. Streams run through the valley, and in places they drop over low waterfalls that locals use as swimming holes in the heat of summer. Buffalo graze the paddy edges, children walk to school along the roadside and the pace of life matches the rhythm of the harvest. Rice is planted in late spring and harvested around September and October, when the terraces turn gold, which is the loveliest time to visit. Many of the families here run homestays, offering a floor mattress under a mosquito net, a shared meal of rice, vegetables and pork, and a drink of corn wine if you wish.

The road is another matter. Surfaces vary from smooth concrete to broken tarmac and mud, particularly after rain, and landslides sometimes block the route in the wet season, which runs from May to September. Corners are blind, and water buffalo, motorbikes and pigs share the lane. Ride slowly, watch for people, and keep out of the way of lorries. Leave time to stop, since the valley's pleasures lie in stopping.

Fuel is available in small roadside shops, though supplies are limited, and it is wise to fill up in the main towns. Ha Giang city, the provincial capital, is the nearest large town and has proper stations and services. Bring cash, since cards are rarely accepted, and a rain jacket, because showers come quickly. The evening meal, around a low table, with talk through gestures and smiles, is one of the best parts of the day.
t.hanoi@21.0,105.9:
Hanoi starts the day with a roar, and the best advice is to join it calmly. This is a city of millions on the Red River, with more motorbikes than anyone has bothered to count, and the Old Quarter, with its thirty-six old guild streets named after the goods once sold there, is the loud, charming core. Hoàn Kiếm lake in the middle is where people jog, practise tai chi and sit eating ice cream at dusk, and the little Ngoc Son temple on its island is joined to the shore by a red wooden bridge.

Leaving by motorcycle is a skill in itself. Traffic flows like a river, with no gaps, and the rule is to hold your line and let others work around you. Sudden stops are what cause trouble. Cross the Red River by the long steel Long Biên bridge, built by the French in the early twentieth century and now for bikes, trains and pedestrians, and you soon reach the flatter, greener country of the delta, with rice fields, duck ponds and brick kilns. Pagodas hide among trees, such as Con Sơn, a Buddhist site in the hills of Hải Dương province where the Trúc Lâm tradition has a major centre. Roads are mostly decent but busy with trucks, so go at a steady pace.

Take time for the city's culture. The Temple of Literature, founded in 1070, was Vietnam's first university and is one of the calmest places in the capital, its courtyards lined with stone tortoises carrying the names of successful scholars. The food is its own reason for being here. Breakfast pho, with clear beef broth and rice noodles, is standard, bún chả of grilled pork and noodles is the lunch of choice, and egg coffee, whisked into a thick cream and poured over strong Vietnamese coffee, is a local invention worth trying.

Hanoi has every sort of service imaginable, from petrol on almost every corner, to repair workshops that can fix a bike by the roadside in minutes. The weather is the main variable: the humid, hot summer from May to September is wet, and winter can be grey and drizzly and cooler than visitors expect. October and November, and spring, are the sweet spots.
t.jiangzhou district@22.5,107.6:
Jiangzhou is the district that holds the city of Chongzuo, in the far southwest of Guangxi, close to the Vietnamese border. The landscape is classic Guangxi karst, with steep, isolated limestone hills that jut from flat green plains like the backs of sleeping animals. Between them the Zuo River winds slowly through sugarcane fields, and the whole region is one of the largest sugar-producing areas in China. The climate is subtropical, warm and wet in summer, mild in winter, and often hazy with mist in the mornings.

Chongzuo is not a tourist town, and that is part of its interest. It is a working, practical place, with markets full of sugarcane, bananas, dragon fruit and longan, and a cuisine shaped by the Zhuang people, who make up the majority of the population in this part of Guangxi and have their own language and festivals. The Zhuang are the largest minority group in China, and the songs and bronze drums of their culture are part of what the nearby rock art preserves. Rice noodles and grilled river fish are easy to find, and the tea here is strong.

Nature is the draw outside the city. The Chongzuo Ecological Park protects the white-headed langur, a rare primate found only in a small area of southern Guangxi, and is one of the few places where it can be seen in karst forest. Farther west, the Detian waterfall on the Vietnam border spills over wide terraces in a broad, thunderous curtain. The roads between these places run through cane fields and past small villages, with views of karst peaks at nearly every bend.

A practical note matters here. Foreign visitors cannot simply bring a motorcycle into China or ride one on a foreign license, because Chinese registration and a Chinese driving permit are required, and most travelers use guided tours or local arrangements instead. Anyone planning to ride should check the rules with a qualified guide before committing.

The towns of the region have all the usual services, with fuel stations along the main roads and plenty of simple restaurants. Roads can be wet in summer, when heavy downpours and typhoon remnants cross the coast. The best seasons are autumn and winter, when the air is cooler and dry and the fields are golden.
t.longhzou county rock art@22.4,107.1:
The great cliff painting here is known as Huashan, which means Flower Mountain, and it is part of the Zuojiang Huashan Rock Art Cultural Landscape, inscribed by UNESCO in 2016. It lies along the Ming River, a tributary of the Zuo, in the karst country of southwest Guangxi near Ningming. On a limestone cliff about two hundred meters wide and rising high above the water, thousands of red figures are painted in iron-rich pigment, showing people with raised arms, bent knees, swords and drums, and dogs among them. The shapes have lasted for roughly two thousand years, protected by an overhang and the dryness of the rock.

The painters are thought to be ancestors of the Zhuang, the Luoyue people, who lived along these rivers between about the fifth century BC and the second century AD. They made the paintings during rituals that probably involved bronze drums, which are still an important symbol in the region. Large figures, with their arms raised and knees bent, appear to be leaders, with smaller ones around them. Seeing them from a boat, as most visitors do, gives a feeling of looking at a crowd frozen in a dance.

The landscape is the second half of the experience. The river is wide, green and slow, bordered by steep karst hills with bamboo along the banks and the occasional water buffalo. Mornings are often misty, and the best light for photographs comes before the sun gets high. In the rainy season, the water rises and the colors of the painting change, with the rock appearing wetter and the figures a darker red.

For riders, a caution is necessary. China does not allow foreign visitors to ride their own motorcycles or use a foreign license on public roads, so independent touring requires special arrangements with a local operator. The nearest large town on the map, Baihe, is a good thirty kilometers away, and for a visit most people reach the site from Ningming or Chongzuo, where there are fuel stations, hotels and restaurants.

The boat trip takes a few hours, and it is wise to bring water and sun protection. The humidity is high in summer. Winter is clearer and cooler, and the paintings are easier to see in the soft light.
t.ha giang base@22.8,105.0:
Ha Giang is the last real town before Vietnam runs out of road and turns into limestone, a small, busy provincial capital on the Lo river, about as far north as you can go without crossing into China. About thirty thousand people live here, in a grid of shops, cafes, homestays and motorbike rental places that exist because of the ride that begins at the edge of town. This is where riders sleep, sort out their kit and eat a big bowl of pho before the mountains, and it is a sensible base for exactly that purpose.

The Ha Giang Loop is the draw, a few days of tight, steep, foggy mountain road through the Dong Van Karst Plateau Geopark. The road climbs from the valley through the Heaven's Gate pass at Quan Ba, past terraced rice fields and villages of the Hmong, Dao and Tay people, to Yen Minh, Dong Van and the border country at Lung Cu, where a flag tower stands at Vietnam's northernmost point. The highlight is the Ma Pi Leng Pass, a narrow shelf cut into a cliff above the Nho Que river, which runs a startling jade green at the bottom of one of the deepest canyons in Southeast Asia. The tarmac is mostly decent but narrow, with sharp hairpins, sudden potholes, mist and the odd buffalo. Take it slowly, and avoid riding at night.

The pass was built by hand in the early 1960s. Thousands of volunteers, many of them young people from across northern Vietnam and from local minority communities, worked with picks and dynamite for years to carve the road from the rock, and it became a symbol of national effort. Near Sa Phin, a short ride off the main route, stands the old palace of a Hmong chieftain family, a house of stone and wood from the early twentieth century. Markets in the hill towns, on certain days of the week, are colourful gatherings where people trade in traditional dress, and the weekly Sunday market in Dong Van draws crowds.

The landscape is spectacular. Stone peaks rise from the fields like broken teeth, and terraces of rice, maize and buckwheat climb the slopes, with pink buckwheat flowers in October and November, and plum blossom in late winter. The air is cool, damp and smells of wood smoke, and the mist often hides everything until it suddenly lifts.

Fuel is easy to find in town, so fill up before leaving. Pack a rain jacket, warm layers and a phone with offline maps, and make sure your bike and brakes are in good order. Beds in town are cheap and simple, and an early night is wise.
t.dong van plateau@23.3,105.4:
The Dong Van plateau is a landscape in which almost nothing is flat. In the far north of Vietnam, in Ha Giang province near the Chinese border, a vast area of limestone has been uplifted, cracked and worn into jagged grey ridges, deep valleys and pockets of terraced fields, and it is protected as a UNESCO Global Geopark. The rock is old, much of it hundreds of millions of years, and in places it is full of fossils. Maize is grown in little pockets of soil between boulders, with farmers building stone walls to hold the earth in place, so that whole hillsides look like handmade quilts.

People live here, too, in a way that seems impossible. The area is home to several ethnic minorities, including the Hmong, Lo Lo, Tay and Dao, and each has its own dress, language and customs. Villages are built of stone and clay, with thick walls against the cold, and the Sunday market in the little town of Dong Van is a riot of colour, with traditional clothing, livestock and food. In autumn, usually October and November, the buckwheat fields bloom with pink and white flowers, a gentle contrast with the grey rock.

The riding is among the best in Southeast Asia. Roads climb and twist along cliffs, with hairpins, sudden drops, steep gradients and stunning views at every bend, and the famous Ma Pi Leng Pass looks down into the Nho Que river canyon, a deep green gash far below. Surface quality is mostly good, but landslides, potholes and fog can be a problem, particularly in the wet season. Traffic is usually light, but trucks, motorbikes and buffalo share the road, and drivers overtake on blind bends, so caution and a steady pace are wise.

The town of Dong Van has fuel, basic guesthouses and simple restaurants, and it is the practical base on the plateau. Elsewhere, fuel may be sold from bottles at roadside shops, so fill up when you can. Try thang co, a traditional horse or buffalo stew, and corn wine, and expect cold nights even in summer, since the altitude is well above a thousand metres. Bring a warm layer and a rain jacket, and give yourself time, because the best moments are often the unplanned stops.
t.thi tran tam son@23.1,105.0:
Climb out of Hà Giang on the QL4C and the first big reward comes at around 1,500 metres, at Quản Bạ, where the road crests a pass known as Heaven's Gate and the karst country of the far north opens in front of you. From the viewpoint you look down onto Tam Sơn, the district town, in a broad valley of rice and corn fields, and beyond it two small, perfectly rounded hills sit side by side. The locals call them the Fairy Bosom, and once you have seen them, you will not need it explained.

The legend goes that a fairy came down from heaven and fell in love with a local H'Mông boy, and when she was called back to the sky, she left her breasts behind to feed their child. The story is told with a wink, but the hills are a genuine sight, especially in the morning when mist lies in the valley and the sun catches their tops. Tam Sơn itself is a small, busy market town, the first real stop after Hà Giang, with a few homestays, guesthouses, cafes and noodle shops.

The landscape changes here. Up to now the road has followed rivers and valleys; from Quản Bạ onwards you are on the edge of the Đồng Văn Karst Plateau, a huge area of limestone peaks, deep valleys and rocky fields where farmers grow corn between the stones. The people are mostly H'Mông, Tày, Dao and other ethnic minorities, and you will see women in embroidered skirts and children walking home from school along the road. The area is poor, and life is hard, but people are friendly and often curious about passing riders.

The riding is spectacular but demanding. The QL4C is a narrow mountain road with endless hairpins, steep gradients and sheer drops, and the surface varies from good tarmac to potholes and gravel. Trucks, buses and local motorbikes share the road, and some drive fast and in the middle. In the rainy season, from May to September, landslides can block the road, and fog can reduce visibility to a few metres. The best time to ride is from October to April, when the skies are clearer and the buckwheat flowers bloom pink and white in late autumn.

Fuel is available in Tam Sơn and in Yên Minh, the next town, but stations can be few and far between beyond, so keep your tank topped up. Try the local corn wine, but only at the end of the day.
t.thi tran ong van@23.3,105.4:
Đồng Văn is the town at the top of the loop, a small market centre high on the karst plateau, close to the Chinese border, and the place most riders spend a night. It sits in a bowl surrounded by limestone peaks, and its heart is an old quarter of traditional houses with mud walls, wooden doors and tiled roofs, built around a market hall. The houses are a hundred years old or more, and in the evening the lanterns are lit, the cafes fill up and the air smells of woodsmoke and grilled meat.

Every Sunday, the market draws people from the villages for miles around: H'Mông, Lô Lô, Tày, Dao and others, many of them in traditional dress, who come to sell livestock, vegetables, textiles and tools, and to meet friends over bowls of thắng cố, a stew of horse meat and offal that is not for everyone, and glasses of corn wine. It is a colourful and noisy affair, and it starts early. The town has become popular with tourists in recent years, and the old quarter can be busy, but the market is still very much a local event.

The plateau around the town is part of the Đồng Văn Karst Plateau Global Geopark, recognised by UNESCO for its geology: vast expanses of grey limestone, sinkholes, caves and fossil beds, some of them hundreds of millions of years old. About fifteen kilometres west, in the village of Sà Phìn, stands the palace of the Vương family, a H'Mông clan whose leader was the de facto ruler of the region in the early twentieth century and made his fortune from opium. The palace is a fortified house of stone and carved wood, built with the help of Chinese craftsmen, and is open to visitors. To the north, the Lũng Cú flag tower marks the northernmost point of Vietnam.

For riders, the town is a base for exploring the plateau and the start of the famous ride over the Mã Pí Lèng pass to Mèo Vạc. The roads here are narrow and steep, with hairpins, sheer drops and changeable surfaces, and the weather can be cold, especially in winter, when temperatures can drop close to freezing and frost is not uncommon. Đồng Văn has fuel, guesthouses, homestays, cafes and restaurants, and it is a good place to rest, eat and check over the bike before the next stage.
t.near thi tran ong van@23.3,105.4:
Mã Pí Lèng is the reason many people ride the Hà Giang Loop at all. Between Đồng Văn and Mèo Vạc, the road climbs to about 1,500 metres and then runs along the edge of a cliff above the Nho Quế River, which flows through a narrow canyon far below, a ribbon of jade green between walls of grey rock. The view from the top is one of the most famous in Vietnam, and it lives up to the reputation: on a clear day you can see the river snaking through the gorge, terraced fields clinging to the slopes and endless ridges stretching into China.

The name is said to mean "the bridge of the horse's nose" in a local language, a reference to how steep and difficult the pass was to cross on horseback. The road was built by hand in the late 1950s and 1960s by thousands of young volunteers from across the region, who worked with hammers and chisels, hanging on ropes over the cliffs. Many died during its construction, and the road is known as the Road of Happiness, Con Đường Hạnh Phúc. A monument at the top of the pass commemorates their work.

The riding is the stuff of legend: tight hairpins, sheer drops, narrow lanes and some of the most spectacular views anywhere. The tarmac is mostly sound but broken in places, and there are plenty of hazards, including trucks, buses, local motorbikes, livestock and other tourists stopping on the bends to take photos. In the rainy season, from May to September, landslides are common, and fog can make the road dangerous. Take it slowly, stop often, and enjoy the view from the designated viewpoints rather than on the bends.

Down in the canyon, the Tu Sản gorge is one of the deepest in Southeast Asia, and boat trips run on the river from a landing at the bottom, reached by a steep side road. There are a few cafes at the viewpoints on the pass, selling coffee, drinks and snacks, and a skywalk at the top for those who want an even more dramatic view. The best light is in the early morning, when mist fills the canyon, or in the late afternoon, when the sun turns the rocks gold.
t.thi tran meo vac@23.2,105.4:
After the drama of Mã Pí Lèng, the road drops into Mèo Vạc, a district town in a narrow valley surrounded by limestone mountains, and the first thing that hits you is how ordinary it is. It is a working town, not a tourist town: concrete houses, government buildings, a market, schools and a few guesthouses and restaurants. After the cliffs above, it is a relief to slow down, eat a bowl of phở and watch the town go about its business.

Mèo Vạc comes alive on Sundays, when its market draws people from across the district, many of them H'Mông, Lô Lô and Dao, who walk or ride in from villages in the mountains. Cattle, pigs, chickens and horses are bought and sold at the edge of town, and the stalls sell everything from embroidered fabrics to plastic buckets and medicinal herbs. Like Đồng Văn, it is a place where tradition and modern life meet, sometimes awkwardly.

About twenty kilometres south, the village of Khâu Vai hosts a famous love market once a year, on the twenty-seventh day of the third lunar month, usually in April or May. The legend tells of two lovers from rival tribes who could not marry and agreed to meet once a year at this place. Today the market is a festival, attended by people from all over the region and by curious visitors, and it is said that former lovers who married other people come here once a year to meet again.

For riders, Mèo Vạc is a base for exploring the eastern part of the loop, and the starting point for the road south toward Du Già and back to Hà Giang, a quieter and rougher route through remote valleys. The roads around the town are narrow and steep, with endless hairpins, and the surface can be poor. The town has fuel stations, guesthouses, homestays, cafes and restaurants, and it is a good place to stay a night if Đồng Văn is too busy. The nights are cool, even in summer, so bring warm clothes.

The town is also a good place to try the local food: corn wine, smoked buffalo meat and mèn mén, a steamed corn flour dish that is a staple of the H'Mông diet. In the evening, sit at a street stall with a glass of rice wine and watch the mountains turn dark.
t.near lung ho@22.9,105.2:
The southern road back from Mèo Vạc is the half of the loop that many people skip, and they miss out. Around Lũng Hồ and the village of Du Già, a few kilometres west, the country is greener and more enclosed than on the high karst plateau: deep valleys with rice terraces, forested slopes, streams and waterfalls, and scattered villages of Tày and H'Mông houses. It feels more remote, and it is. Fewer tourists come this way, and the homestays are simple and welcoming.

Du Già is known for its waterfall, a short walk from the village, where locals and travellers swim in a cold pool in summer, and for the scenery along the road, which follows a river through a valley of rice fields and limestone hills. In the harvest season, around September and October, the terraces turn gold, and in spring they are flooded and mirror the sky. Life here is quieter than on the plateau, with farming, weaving and raising buffalo, and the people are curious and friendly.

The riding is more challenging than on the main loop. The roads around here are narrow and often rough, with sections of broken tarmac, gravel, mud and river crossings, especially in the rainy season, from May to September. Road works have improved some stretches in recent years, but conditions change quickly after storms. The hairpins are steep and tight, and there are long stretches with no villages at all. This is not a road to ride fast or tired, and an off-road bike or a light scooter is better than a heavy touring machine.

Fuel is the big consideration here. The villages have small shops that sell petrol in bottles, but there are few proper stations between Mèo Vạc, Yên Minh and Hà Giang, so fill up before you set off and carry a spare litre or two if you can. Food is simple: rice, vegetables, pork and eggs, and plenty of local rice wine. The homestays in Du Già offer a bed, a hot meal and often a warm welcome around the fire. The nearest large town with all services is Hà Giang, about twenty-seven kilometres away as the crow flies, but much further by road. The best time to ride is from October to April, when the weather is drier and cooler.
